title: Visitor and Smile
premise: Vesper Eastwick, a pest controller who prides herself on never believing in anything she can't spray, trap, or bill for, takes a routine call at Hollowmere House and finds something with fingerprints that shouldn't have them. The house's mirrors lag a second behind reality, and the lag is growing—because in 1974 the house's former owner stole a year of time from the people who lived there, trapping their echoes inside the glass. Vesper discovers she's the last living descendant of the thief, which means the debt is hers to repay: she must return what was taken by giving the house something it has never had—a genuine act of belonging. In the end, Vesper chooses to stay, trading her invisibility for a found family among the freed echoes, and the mirrors finally reflect her in real time.
about_author: Y. M. Kavanagh spent a decade working property maintenance in decaying English manor houses before turning to fiction full-time. They write horror about ordinary tradespeople stumbling into the extraordinary, insisting the scariest rooms are always the ones someone was paid to fix.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. A routine pest complaint at derelict Hollowmere House; she finds claw marks at ceiling height and small handprints in dust—fingers too long, prints facing inward. She bills the estate manager and leaves. Emotional beat: dry competence masking loneliness.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Called back when the new owner, Priya Chandra, reports 'delays' in the mirrors. Vesper watches her own reflection blink after she does. She blames old glass, faulty wiring, anything. Beat: the first crack in her disbelief.

chapters.title: Inventory of Denial
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. She inspects every mirror with instruments, finds nothing wrong except the lag—now two seconds. She lies to Priya about needing parts. Beat: fear dressed up as professionalism.

chapters.title: Priya
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The young owner inherited Hollowmere from an unknown benefactor and can't afford to leave. She shows Vesper the nursery where the lag is worst. Beat: reluctant connection between two women both pretending they're fine.

chapters.title: What the Dust Remembers
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. In the attic she finds a 1974 ledger: the previous owner, Aldous Wren, recorded 'withdrawals'—days taken from servants' lives. Her own surname appears as witness. Beat: dread of inheritance.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. The thing in the walls leaves prints matching her own. It's been following her since chapter one. She catches its reflection moving independently. Beat: belief arrives not as revelation but as nausea.

chapters.title: The Servants' Stair
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya descends stairs that weren't there yesterday into a mirrored corridor where figures wait without faces. One wears a maid's uniform and mouths Vesper's name. Beat: awe curdling into protectiveness.

chapters.title: Family Tree
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Records show Aldous Wren took a year from four servants in 1974; his daughter, Vesper's grandmother, helped him do it and fled with the guilt. The debt passed down. Beat: rage at bloodlines.

chapters.title: Three Seconds
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. The lag spreads beyond mirrors—to windows, to her phone camera, to her own memory arriving late. She nearly drives away but turns back for Priya. Beat: choosing someone over safety.

chapters.title: The Maid's Name
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Researching, Priya identifies the trapped servant: Edith Marlowe, dismissed pregnant in 1974, erased from records. Her echo has been waiting fifty years to be acknowledged. Beat: grief for the unrecorded.

chapters.title: Negotiation
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Vesper speaks aloud to the house, offering to return the stolen year. The mirrors answer by showing 1974—the taking, in full, from Edith's perspective. Beat: horror as testimony.

chapters.title: Aldous Wren's Study
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. She finds Wren's mechanism: a clockwork device that siphoned time, still ticking behind the study wall. Destroying it would free nothing—the time must be returned willingly by his heir. Beat: the trap of legacy.

chapters.title: Invisible No More
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The house begins claiming Priya as substitute payment. Veper realizes staying invisible—never signing leases, never committing—was how she dodged debts all her life. Now her name is required. Beat: identity as liability and gift.

chapters.title: Edith
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Vesper enters the mirror corridor and meets Edith's echo face to face. Edith doesn't want revenge; she wants her lost year back—her daughter's first steps, held somewhere in the glass. Beat: compassion replacing terror.

chapters.title: The Price of a Year
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Returning the year requires a living heir to give a year of their own. Priya volunteers; Vesper refuses to let her. Their argument becomes the book's emotional core about what family owes. Beat: love tested by arithmetic.

chapters.title: Wren's Ghost
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Aldous's echo appears, unrepentant, arguing power is meant to be used. He offers Vesper the device instead—take time, don't give it. Beat: temptation articulated seductively.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Vesper smashes the ledger, renounces the inheritance, and declares herself Edith's family instead of Wren's. The corridor shudders; the house must decide whose claim holds. Beat: defiance as turning point.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Pulled into the past, Vesper witnesses the taking and, crucially, the moment her grandmother could have stopped it and didn't. She understands corruption as a series of small permissions. Beat: inherited shame confronted.

chapters.title: The Giving
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Climax. Vesper offers her year—not as payment but as belonging, asking Edith to share it rather than replace it. The device shatters; the mirrors flood with light; the echoes step through. Beat: sacrifice reframed as welcome.

chapters.title: Afterimages
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The house exhales. Edith, aged one year, alive and real, walks out holding photographs of a life restored. The other echoes disperse into peace. Beat: release and wonder.

chapters.title: Hollowmere, Occupied
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Weeks later: Vesper signs the lease, hangs her tools in the mudroom, teaches Edith to use a phone. The mirrors reflect instantly, faithfully. Beat: domesticity as hard-won victory.

chapters.title: Visitor and Smile
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. A new visitor arrives with a pest complaint—and a lagging pocket watch. Vesper smiles, believes now, and opens the door wide. Beat: the invisible woman becomes the one who answers.
